L0@P0: EVALUATION OF BREFCOR BRDF EFFECTS CORRECTION FOR HYSPEX, CASI, AND
L1@P0: APEX IMAGING SPECTROSCOPY DATA
L2@P0: Daniel Schlapfer ¨
L3@P0: ReSe Applications
L4@P0: Langeggweg 3, 9500 Wil, Switzerland
L5@P0: daniel@rese.ch
L6@P0: Rudolf Richter
L7@P0: German Aerospace Center (DLR)
L8@P0: DE-82234 Wessling, Germany
L9@P0: rudolf.richter@dlr.de
L10@P0: ABSTRACT
L11@P0: The correction of BRDF effects for airborne wide FOV imaging spectroscopy data is of interest for a consistent data processing and products generation. Recently, a new BRDF effects correction method (BREFCOR) has been implemented
L12@P0: as additional processing step after the well-known atmospheric compensation workflow. This paper shows validation
L13@P0: results of the method for sample data sets of HYSPEX, CASI,
L14@P0: and APEX data. It can be shown that the method is able to
L15@P0: deal with a broad variety of sensors and surface characteristics. The quality of the spectral albedo data products is
L16@P0: substantially increased in terms of consistency for all data
L17@P0: sets. Future potential improvements and additions for a better operational usability and for the processing of complete
L18@P0: spectra are finally summarized.
L19@P0: Index Terms— Atmospheric Correction, ATCOR, BREFCOR, BRDF, Radiometric correction, HYSPEX, CASI,
L20@P0: APEX.
L21@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L22@P0: Airborne optical scanners are able to provide measurements
L23@P0: of the at-sensor radiance accurate to a level of 2-3% in absolute radiance units. These radiance values are converted to
L24@P0: bottom of atmosphere reflectance values, mostly by inverting the radiative transfer using an atmospheric compensation
L25@P0: package such as ATCOR-4 [1]. In a first order, this output
L26@P0: quantity is a not-well defined reflectance quantity as it depends on the angular distribution of the illumination field, the
L27@P0: main solar incidence angles and the observation angle. By
L28@P0: improved treatment of the solar irradiance field for the diffuse and the direct component and the terrain influences, and
L29@P0: by taking into account the relative solar incidence angle on
L30@P0: a per pixel basis, the reflectance may be modeled closer to
L31@P0: the ideal situation of a true isotropic hemispherical irradiance field [2]. Taking these additions and assumptions into
L32@P0: account, we may describe the output of the atmospheric correction as a hemispheric directional reflectance factor (HDRF,
L33@P0: [3]). It is to be noted that the term ”HDRF” is often used in an
L34@P0: ambiguous way as it is also used for a description of the geometric situation regardless of the distribution of the illumination field across the hemisphere; we use the original physical
L35@P0: definition where an isotropic irradiance field is a precondition of any HDRF value. The observation direction, i.e., the
L36@P0: second direction of the bidirectional reflectance distribution
L37@P0: function BRDF [3] is still to be corrected after this processing as the HDRF values may deviate relative to the average
L38@P0: spectral albedo by up to 50% [4, 5].
L39@P0: Recently, a novel correction method has been implemented within the framework of the ATCOR-4 atmospheric
L40@P0: correction solution. We name it the BREFCOR ’BRDF effects correction’ method. The method uses the Ross-Li sparse
L41@P0: reciprocal BRDF model which is tuned based on a continuous surface cover characterization index. This allows to get
L42@P0: a surface cover dependent but yet continuous correction of
L43@P0: the HDRF to bihemispherical reflectance (BHR), i.e., to the
L44@P0: spectral albedo. The method is of generic nature and has been
L45@P0: successfully applied to 4-band photogrammetric imagery as
L46@P0: well as to multispectral space borne multi-angle imagery. In
L47@P0: this paper, we focus on the use of BREFCOR with imaging
L48@P0: spectroscopy data. Firstly, we shortly summarize the principles of the method. Secondly, we’ll show sample results
L49@P0: for three imaging spectroscopy data sets from three different
L50@P0: sensors and surface characteristics by analyzing the spectra
L51@P0: in overlap regions of adjacent image lines. Validation is done
L52@P0: on the level of spectral albedo which is the basis for a broad
L53@P0: variety of imaging spectroscopy applications.
L54@P0: 2. THE BREFCOR METHOD - OVERVIEW
L55@P0: The BREFCOR method which is used in this paper is part of
L56@P0: the ATCOR atmospheric correction process. It is described
L57@P0: in detail in [6] and [7]. The BRDF effects correction is applied subsequently to the atmospheric compensation to convert the hemispherical-directional reflectances to observationangle independent spectral albedo. The idea is to apply a scaling of the volume scattering and the geometric scattering of
L58@P0-1: the surface cover using a well accepted BRDF model. A fuzzysurface characterization index which we call the BRDF cover
L59@P1: index (BCI) is used for this purpose. The index covers all
L60@P1: surface types from water to asphalt and concrete, soils, sparse
L61@P1: vegetation and dense vegetation as a unified continuous index. This parameter is formed by extension of the NDVI
L62@P1: to both, non-vegetated and densely vegetated surfaces. The
L63@P1: Ross-Li-sparse reciprocal BRDF model is used as the basis
L64@P1: for the correction of reflectance anisotropy [8]. The model
L65@P1: is calibrated for the various surface types by estimating the
L66@P1: best fitting kernel weight values. In summary, the BREFCOR
L67@P1: correction procedure consists of the following steps:
L68@P1: • perform atmospheric compensation to bottom of atmosphere HDRF,
L69@P1: • calculate scene-specific kernels reduced to the image’s
L70@P1: solar zenith and relative azimuth angle range,
L71@P1: • calculate the BCI from image and aggregate in 4 to 7
L72@P1: discrete classes,
L73@P1: • calibrate the BRDF-model for all classes and scenes
L74@P1: (i.e., find the kernel weighting factors),
L75@P1: • create a best suited model by combining all image
L76@P1: scenes of the processing,
L77@P1: • calculate a spectral anisotropy map using the continuous BCI applied to the calibrated BRDF model and the
L78@P1: observation angles for each image pixel,
L79@P1: • applicate the anisotropy to the imagery on a per-pixel
L80@P1: basis.
L81@P1: The final product is a spectral albedo image cube corrected for observation BRDF effects. Hereafter, some sample
L82@P1: outputs of this process for three kind of imaging spectrometers are shown.
L83@P1: 3. EVALUATION ON HYSPEX IMAGERY
L84@P1: The method has been applied to Hyspex imagery [9]. The
L85@P1: sample data was acquired over the Kaufbeuren test site in
L86@P1: Southern Germany on the 8th of July 2013; the sun was at 41◦
L87@P1: zenith and 113◦azimuth angle. The Hyspex imaging spectroscopy system scans the surface with a total FOV of 34◦
L88@P1: in
L89@P1: 160 contiguous bands for the VNIR spectral range from 410
L90@P1: to 990 nm. The BRDF model is calibrated for each of the 160
L91@P1: spectral bands individually using 5 steps with calibration limits for dense summer vegetation. One of the scenes contained
L92@P1: some clouds and had therefore to be excluded from the model
L93@P1: calibration step. A result of this correction is shown in Figure
L94@P1: 1. BRDF effects are well removed for both the grassland and
L95@P1: forested areas.
L96@P1: A collection of spectra which illustrate the effect of the

L98@P1: spectra averages from a 10x10 pixel window of the same
L99@P1: target viewn from two different observation angles in the
L100@P1: overlapping area of the mosaicked images (see red dots in
L101@P1: Figure 2). The BRDF effects are strongly reduced for the
L102@P1: Fig. 1. BRDF correction on Hyspex: left: ATCOR corrected,
L103@P1: middle: BREFCOR corrected, right: anisotropy factor. Band
L104@P1: combination: R:803nm, G:546nm, and B:426nm.
L105@P1: Fig. 2. Spectra of three surface types at edge of image before
L106@P1: and after BREFCOR correction.

L108@P1: average difference in reflectance from 2.5% to below 1%.
L109@P1: The concrete sample is hardly affected by the correction as it
L110@P1: it shows only small BRDF anisotropy.

L112@P1: A second evaluation was done on a CASI-1500 VNIR data set

L122@P2: in more pronounced BRDF effects as seen in the previous imagery. The underlying digital elevation model stems from
L123@P2: ASTER imagery. ATCOR correction was performed with a
L124@P2: 60 km visibility. Due to the reduced accuracy of the DEM,
L125@P2: the terrain influences could only be roughly corrected, resulting in small scale irradiance variations still being visible in
L126@P2: the outputs. An overall BRDF correction function has been
L127@P2: found by combined analyses of all strips. The resulting mosaic is shown in Figure 3; the across track variations could be
L128@P2: significantly reduced using this model based BRDF correction.
L129@P2: If comparing the spectra from two observation angles in
L130@P2: the overlap region (see red dots in Figure 3) , a significant
L131@P2: portion of the BRDF effects is corrected with the BREFCOR
L132@P2: method (see Figure 4). The correction reduces the BRDF
L133@P2: effects from an average of 2-3.9% reflectance difference to
L134@P2: 1.3-1.9%. The remaining artifacts can most probably be attributed to the insufficient correction of terrain influences by
L135@P2: the coarse DEM involved in this image processing. For vegetation, the correction is less significant as only a small portion
